opus-5.5.text:
I think they're complementary. They solve different parts of the same problem, so the question is how to divide the labor.

Linear attention, or more broadly the RNN-style layers like Gated DeltaNet, compresses the whole history into a fixed-size state. That's great for efficiency and for things like state tracking, but it's lossy. When you need precise retrieval, like finding a specific token from 100K tokens ago, a fixed-size state struggles. That's why hybrid models keep some full-attention layers, maybe one in every four or eight.

But those full-attention layers are still quadratic. Once the linear layers have made everything else cheap, the remaining full-attention layers dominate the cost at long context. So the natural move is to make those global layers sparse. Instead of attending to every token, each query selects a small subset of relevant blocks or tokens, as in NSA or DeepSeek's DSA-style approaches.

So my ideal architecture has three pieces:
- **Linear or delta-rule layers** do most of the work. They handle local and compositional processing and keep a compressed summary of the past.
- **A few sparse attention layers** replace dense attention. They act as a precise retrieval mechanism, like a lookup into memory.
- **Possibly sliding-window attention** for local precision, although a good linear layer with short convolutions already covers much of that.

The interesting research question is whether the layers can inform each other. The recurrent state already contains a summary of what's in the context, so in principle it could help decide which blocks the sparse layer should retrieve. Right now most designs just stack the layers and let training figure it out. I think a tighter coupling, where the compressed memory guides the sparse lookup, is where things could get really elegant.

There's also the hardware side, which I care a lot about. Sparse attention only helps in practice if the selection is block-structured and kernel-friendly. Otherwise you save FLOPs on paper and lose them to memory access. So whatever combination we choose has to be co-designed with efficient kernels from the start. Hybrid linear attention plus block-sparse global attention seems like the most promising direction for long-context models right now.

r001.rationale: The response says sparse attention layers should replace dense full-attention layers and make the global layers sparse.

r002.rationale: It proposes sparse layers as replacements but does not state that they could fully replace a full-attention layer conditional on accurate token selection.

r003.rationale: It discusses kernel and memory-access limitations, but not inaccurate token selection as a major limitation.

r004.rationale: It does not mention DeepSeek’s DSC or distillation to improve an indexer’s selection accuracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of them as competing options; I see them as attacking different parts of the same problem. Hybrid attention is about changing the ratio: most layers become linear attention or some other recurrent form with a fixed-size state, and you keep only a small number of full-attention layers, say one in every seven or eight. Those few layers are what preserve exact retrieval, in-context copying, and the things we know a compressed state fundamentally can't do well. But those remaining layers are still quadratic, and at very long context they end up dominating both compute and KV-cache memory, so you haven't really escaped the problem, you've just divided it by a constant.

That's exactly where sparse attention belongs. So my ideal design is: the linear or recurrent layers carry the bulk of the modeling capacity cheaply, and the few global layers you keep are made sparse rather than dense. You don't need full attention there because the recurrent layers already summarize the local and medium-range context quite well. What the global layers need to do is pick out the small number of tokens that actually matter for precise recall. Something like NSA-style compression plus token selection, or block-sparse retrieval over the KV cache, fits that role very naturally. In a sense the recurrent layers can even help you decide what to select, since they've already built a summary of the sequence.

There are two things I would pay attention to. One is that the sparse layers should be trainable end-to-end rather than bolted on after the fact, because the model has to learn to route information through them. The other is hardware: both linear attention and sparse attention are only worth it if the kernels are actually efficient, so I'd want block-level sparsity that maps cleanly onto the memory hierarchy, not fine-grained patterns that look good on paper and run slowly in practice. If you get those right, you end up with something that is close to linear in cost but keeps most of the retrieval ability of a dense transformer, which is really the goal.

r001.rationale: It proposes making the few retained global layers sparse rather than dense.

r002.rationale: It says full attention is unnecessary in those layers if they can select the small number of tokens needed for precise recall.

r003.rationale: It discusses selecting relevant tokens but does not identify inaccurate selection as a major limitation of current sparse attention.

r004.rationale: It does not mention DeepSeek’s DSC, distillation, or improving an indexer’s selection accuracy.

astra-6.text:
I’d think of them as complementary. Hybrid attention lets you combine different kinds of attention across layers, while sparse attention lets you reduce how much context a particular layer has to look at.

So one approach would be to use a cheap local or linear attention mechanism in most layers, and then use sparse global attention in selected layers. The local mechanism handles nearby dependencies, and the sparse global mechanism retrieves relevant information from farther back in the context. You might retain a few full-attention layers if they’re needed for quality.

The key question is how to choose what to attend to. Ideally, that choice should depend on the input, but the selection itself has to be cheap. If finding the important tokens costs as much as attending to everything, you haven’t gained much. I’d optimize the combination around actual latency and memory use, alongside model quality, rather than sparsity alone.

r002.rationale: It says some full-attention layers might be retained, but does not state that accurate token selection would let sparse attention fully replace a full-attention layer.

r003.rationale: It discusses the cost of selecting tokens, but does not identify inaccurate selection as a major limitation of current sparse attention.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention DeepSeek’s DSC, distillation, or improving an indexer’s selection accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d combine them by using sparse attention for precise retrieval and a linear or recurrent component for maintaining broader context. The recurrent component gives you an efficient summary of the history, while sparse attention lets you go back to specific tokens when that summary isn’t enough.

The interesting question is how to make those components work together. Ideally, the model would learn when it needs exact information and which parts of the context to retrieve, rather than following a fixed sparse pattern. You’d also want the selection mechanism to be cheap; otherwise, you can lose the efficiency you gained from sparsity.

So I’d start with a simple hybrid architecture, then make its attention component sparse. The goal would be to preserve the ability to retrieve details over long contexts while keeping most of the computation efficient.

r001.rationale: The response proposes starting with a hybrid architecture and making its attention component sparse, while a recurrent component maintains broader context.

r002.rationale: It does not say sparse attention could fully replace a full-attention layer if token selection is accurate.

r003.rationale: It discusses making token selection cheap and adaptive, but does not identify inaccurate selection as a major limitation.

r004.rationale: It does not mention DeepSeek’s DSC, distillation, or improving an indexer’s token-selection accuracy.
